task: Write one sentence of your own using the word plethora. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know plethora should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Grandma's junk drawer holds a plethora of keys — decades of them — though no one can name a single lock they open.
Plenty stops short of plethora — plenty is comfortably enough, while a plethora is already more than anyone asked for.
Glut goes further than plethora — a plethora crowds the shelf, but a glut breaks the system, burying prices, patience, or both.

Oversupply is the economist's word for a market where supply has outrun demand — warehouses filling because buyers stopped buying. A plethora needs no market at all: it is the livelier, everyday word for a pile of too many, from passwords to remote controls.

A deluge is abundance arriving as a flood — applications, emails, complaints pouring in faster than anyone can respond, the emphasis all on the rush of arrival. A plethora is what remains once everything has landed: the standing pile of more than anyone can use.
less than what was counted on
an absence where something is needed

Greek plethein, 'to be full,' is distant kin to Latin plenus (the root behind plenty), but the Greek line left no other everyday English word — plethora stands alone, a doctor's term that escaped the clinic. Its plural, if you ever need one, is plethoras, not some Greek flourish.
Plethora means an abundance, excess.
The new hires' welcome packet contained a plethora of passwords: badge codes, parking codes, seven single-use logins, and a printed warning not to write any of them down.
Plethora began as a doctor's diagnosis — an excess of blood — and the word still carries a symptom's edge: not just many, but more than is useful, an abundance that starts to get in the way.
A plethora is rarely a pure compliment: the word counts past 'plenty' and sighs.
For welcome abundance this unit gives you plenitude; for the harmful extreme, surfeit or glut.
Reach for plethora when the pile itself is the point — options, emails, remote controls — more than anyone can use.

Marisol signed up for one streaming service in college, mostly for documentaries.
A decade later her budgeting app tells a different story: eleven subscriptions, four of them free trials she forgot to cancel.
Media critics have a name for this stage of the industry -- a plethora of platforms, each with one show worth watching and a fee attached.
The result is a strange kind of paralysis.
Surveys find viewers now spend longer choosing what to watch than watching it.
Marisol's fix was blunt: she canceled everything but two, and says she has not missed a single evening since.
